summary: This proposed standard describes how to extend the ForCES Logical Functional Block topology across forwarding elements by defining the inter-FE LFB class. The class passes data and metadata between forwarding elements without changes to the ForCES specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A router can be built from several parts that need to hand work to each other. This defines a standard handoff so packets and notes pass between parts.

questions: what is the forces inter-fe lfb
how do forces forwarding elements share metadata
what is a logical functional block
subtitle: A standard way to carry packets and their metadata between the forwarding elements of one network device over Ethernet.

tldr.problem: ForCES models packet processing inside one forwarding element as a graph of blocks, but sometimes that processing needs to be split across several forwarding elements, and the metadata has to travel with the packet.
tldr.mechanism: A new LFB class, the inter-FE LFB, wraps the packet and selected metadata in an Ethernet frame with a dedicated ethertype and TLV-encoded metadata, and unwraps it at the receiving FE.
tldr.outcome: The graph of blocks can span multiple forwarding elements without any change to the ForCES specification itself. It focuses on Ethernet and is meant for a single private network.

today: RFC 8013 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the ForCES model of RFC 5812 and the LFB library of RFC 6956.

sections.title: Extending ForCES Across Forwarding Elements
sections.content:
In the ForCES architecture, a packet service is modeled as a graph of Logical Functional Block (LFB) instances inside a single Forwarding Element (FE). A Control Element (CE) sets up that processing sequence and the parameters of each block. Blocks already pass metadata to each other along with the packet.

Sometimes it helps to spread this processing across more than one FE, either to scale out or to use specialized hardware on particular FEs. This RFC defines how to do that by adding a new LFB class, the inter-FE LFB, without needing any changes to the ForCES definitions. It focuses on Ethernet as the link between FEs.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside a machine, workers pass a package along a line and scribble notes on it. This lets the line continue into a second machine without losing the notes.

sections.title: Scope and Use Cases
sections.content:
The problem is passing ForCES-defined metadata alongside packet data across FEs, which may be physical or virtual. The RFC assumes the FEs belong to the same Network Element, sit in a single administrative private network in close proximity, and are already connected by Ethernet. Other transports, such as UDP over IP, are not addressed.

Two examples show the need. In a basic IPv4 router, the chain is an ingress LFB, an IPv4 validator, an IPv4 unicast longest-prefix-match LFB, an IPv4 next-hop LFB and an egress LFB. It can be split into two FEs after the LPM block, so the packet and its ingress and next-hop metadata must cross between them. The second example is a chain of network functions, such as deep packet inspection, NAT and routing, that can be split across three FEs for scale-out or because different vendors supply different functions.

The RFC notes that proprietary interconnects exist for carrying packet and metadata between FEs, and defines a standard mechanism instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a long assembly line cut in two parts placed in different rooms. The sticky notes on each item must still reach the second room.

sections.title: The Inter-FE LFB Design
sections.content:
The design choice was to define a normal LFB class rather than change the core ForCES architecture. An alternative would have required changes to the FE Object capabilities (SupportedLFBs) and the LFBTopology component.

The inter-FE LFB sits at the cut point in the graph. On the source FE, the egress side receives the raw packet and metadata. Its inputs carry a unique set of selection information, and it uses them to pick the encapsulation details: the source and destination FEs (abstracted as MAC addresses) and which metadata to pass along. On the destination FE, the ingress side uses the received frame to decide which LFB instance continues the processing and which metadata to hand over. In the router example, the receiving side feeds the IPv4 next-hop LFB.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender desk packs the item and notes into an envelope addressed to the next room. A receiver desk opens it and gives the item to the right worker.

sections.title: The Ethernet Encapsulation
sections.content:
The wire format is an Ethernet frame. After the destination and source MAC addresses comes the inter-FE ethertype, a 16-bit metadata length, and then the TLV-encoded metadata, followed by the original packet data. The resulting frame is 32-bit aligned.

  • The destination MAC address identifies the destination FE, and the source MAC address the source FE, as set by CE policy.
  • The ethertype ED3E (hexadecimal) identifies an inter-FE LFB frame.
  • The metadata length counts all encoded metadata, including the 16 bits of the length field itself.
  • Each metadatum is a TLV whose type is the ForCES metadata ID registered with IANA. Every TLV is 32-bit aligned, with zero padding if needed.

A 16-bit TLV limits metadata IDs to 16 bits, rather than the 32-bit ForCES component ID space. The authors judged this sufficient, and the TLV form saves 4 bytes per metadatum compared with an Index-Length-Value (ILV) form.
sections.plainLanguage: The envelope has a to-and-from address, a special stamp saying it is an inter-machine envelope, a note about how long the notes section is, then the notes, then the original package.

sections.title: Egress and Ingress Processing
sections.content:
The LFB has two input port groups, EgressInGroup and IngressInGroup, and three outputs: OUT1 (the encapsulated frame), OUT2 (the decapsulated packet plus metadata) and EXCEPTIONOUT (an exception ID, the packet and metadata).

Egress. The LFB maps the incoming port to a row of the IFETable. If the lookup works, it increments statistics, applies the optional metadata filter list (a whitelist of metadata to send), checks that the extra header and metadata will not exceed the MTU, builds the Ethernet header from the DSTFE and SRCFE fields, uses the optional IFETYPE as ethertype (or ED3E if absent), wraps each allowed metadatum in a TLV and updates the metadata length. A failed lookup or no allowed metadata sends the data to EXCEPTIONOUT with EncapTableLookupFailed. If the MTU would be exceeded, it uses FragRequired.

Ingress. A frame is recognized by its ethertype and optionally its MAC addresses. The LFB walks the TLVs, accepting metadata allowed by the row's filter. Unknown or disallowed metadata IDs are ignored, the error count is incremented and processing continues. It then skips the inter-FE header to reconstruct the original packet and passes it, with the metadata, downstream. The EXCEPTIONOUT port is an abstraction, and an implementation may simply drop packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender checks its address book, packs only the allowed notes, and sends the envelope. The receiver reads the notes it knows about, ignores strange ones and hands over the original package.

sections.title: Components and the XML Model
sections.content:
The CE accesses two components. IFETable is a read-write array populated by the CE. Each row is an IFEInfo structure with an optional IFETYPE, an optional StatId, the destination MAC (DSTFE), the source MAC (SRCFE) and an optional MetaFilterList of allowed metadata IDs. IFEStats is read-only, populated by the FE, and holds byte, packet and error counts. Because StatId is optional, an implementation may link table rows to statistics rows through it, at provisioning time, or by using the row index.

The RFC gives the full XML definition of the LFB library. IANA registered it as LFB class identifier 18, name IFE, version 1.0. The RFC also requests a new Ethernet protocol type from IEEE.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an address book the controller fills in, and a counter sheet the machine fills in to show how many envelopes it handled.

sections.title: MTU, QoS and Congestion
sections.content:
Adding data to Ethernet frames raises MTU issues. The RFC recommends large MTUs such as jumbo frames when possible and limiting the metadata sent. A port can be set to report a lower MTU to upper layers to leave room for metadata, but care is needed: for IPv4 the minimum size is 64 octets and for IPv6 it is 1280 octets.

The inter-FE LFB does not change Class-of-Service semantics, because the CoS marks on the resulting frame are honored downstream. No extra congestion control is specified because most traffic is IP and already congestion controlled. Metadata does add bandwidth need, so traffic engineering SHOULD be done. The LFB MUST be deployed only in a single operator's network or among adjacent cooperating operators, a Controlled Environment, with extra measures such as rate-limiting inter-FE traffic, circuit breaking or isolating it on dedicated interfaces or VLANs.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding notes makes the envelope fatter, so the road between the rooms must be wide enough, and the traffic should stay inside the building.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The FEs are in one Network Element and one private Ethernet LAN, but an implementation SHOULD support MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) for message authentication and optional confidentiality. Keys can be configured manually or through MACsec Key Agreement over IEEE 802.1X EAP, and the RFC expects FEs to start with shared keys from the control plane and move to automated key management.

Security is NE-wide, and operators SHOULD configure the same policy on all FEs. EAP-TLS SHOULD be the EAP method, and strict validation mode SHOULD be used, so non-protected, invalid or unverifiable frames MUST be dropped. The RFC warns that a compromised FE could fake or modify inter-FE traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the envelopes travel on a shared wire inside the building, they can be sealed and signed so nobody can slip in a fake one.

fields.name: Destination MAC Address
fields.desc: Identifies the destination FE by CE policy.

fields.name: Source MAC Address
fields.desc: Identifies the source FE by CE policy.

fields.name: Inter-FE ethertype
fields.desc: Marks the frame as inter-FE LFB type.

fields.name: Metadata length
fields.desc: Total encoded metadata length, including this field.

fields.name: TLV encoded Metadata
fields.desc: One or more 32-bit aligned TLVs, variable length.
